description.narrative: Asia Pacific Forum for Women Law and Development (APWLD) is a regional membership-based organisation including 268 members from 30 countries across the Asia Pacific Region. The aim of the organisation is 1) To strengthen feminist movements at local, national and regional levels and in particular to support the most marginalised women; 2) To amplify the influence, impact and voice of Asia Pacific women´s rights advocates in local, national, regional and global policy setting bodies; 3) To facilitate the production of evidence-based research and tools for advocacy outcomes and movement building; and 4) To build the capacities of women´s rights organisations and movements in the region using right-base perspectives. The stakeholders to the contribution are APWLD´s 268 member organisations and their communities’ representing women from grassroot level and marginalised groups and women at policy level.

Asia Pacific Forum for Women, Law and Development (APWLD) är en regional medlemsbaserad organisation med 268 medlemmar från 30 länder i Asien och Oceanien. Insatsen syftar till 1) att stärka feministiska rörelser på lokal, nationell och regional nivå med särskilt fokus på de mest marginaliserade kvinnorna; 2) att öka deras påverkansmöjligheter i nationella, regionala och globala fora; 3) att stödja evidensbaserad forskning och kvinnorättsorganisationers uppbyggnad och möjlighet till påverkan; och att 4) bygga upp kapaciteten hos kvinnorättsorganisationer och -rörelser i regionen med hjälp av rättighetsbaserade arbetssätt och perspektiv.

In the Strategic Plan (2022-2026), APWLD ´s overall goal is threefold; to promote women´s human rights in the region; to empower women in the Asia Pacific region to use law as an instrument for change for equality, justice, peace and development; and to strengthen womens rights movements and feminist activism across the Asia Pacific Region.
This will be done by focusing on four overarching objectives for the five year period;
1.To strengthen feminist movements at local, national and regional levels and in particular to support the most marginalised women.
2.To amplify the influence, impact and voice of Asia Pacific women´s rights advocates in local, national, regional and global policy setting bodies.
3. To facilitate the production of evidence-based research and tools for advocacy outcomes and movement building; and
4) To build the capacities of women´s rights organisations and movements in the region using rights-based perspectives and intersection of patriarchy, globalisation, fundamentalisms and militarisation.
According to APWLD's Strategic Plan (2022-2026) four overarching objectives will be integrated through eleven integrated programs. These programs cover comprehensive critical challenges in the region including protection on women human right defenders, climate change, labour and decent work, migration, international trade agreements, feminist legal networks and women political leadership.

sector.narrative: Women’s rights organisations and movements, and government institutions

description.narrative:
To strengthen feminist movements at local, national and regional levels and in particular to support the most marginalised women
In 2024, APWLD strengthened feminist movements in the region by engaging more than a thousand women human rights defenders through its thematic networks. Members reported improved ability to coordinate advocacy and respond to shrinking civic space for e.g. in Myanmar APWLD coordinated a rapid solidarity action after the arrest of a womens labour organiser in Yangon, mobilising regional pressure that contributed to her release on bail. In Bangladesh, APWLD supported women workers groups documenting harassment in garment factories, which led to a coalition of unions adopting a joint protocol for responding to genderbased violence at work.
To amplify the influence, impact and voice of Asia Pacific women´s rights advocates in local, national, regional and global policy setting bodies
APWLDs Womens Political Participation (WPP) programme and FPAR cycles enabled women leaders to influence local decisionmaking despite shrinking democratic space. For example in Nepal in 2024 there was a group of Dalit women FPAR researchers that used their findings on water access discrimination to pressure the local ward office to allocate budget for a community water point. This is the first time Dalit women had successfully influenced a local development budget. In the Philippines, women leaders trained by APWLD organised community dialogues on political participation despite ongoing redtagging, resulting in several women being appointed to barangaylevel committees (forum where community members cooperate with local government concerning social services).
To increase influence of feminist perspectives in regional and global policy arenas
APWLD played a visible role in shaping regional and global policy debates. At COP29, APWLD delegates presented communitygenerated evidence on climateinduced displacement, which was cited by civil society coalitions advocating for stronger lossanddamage financing. An example of policy influence occurred at UNESCAPs AsiaPacific Forum on Sustainable Development, where APWLDs submission on feminist development justice was referenced in the civil society joint statement, shaping the final recommendations delivered to member states. In ASEAN processes, APWLDs analysis on migrant women workers informed the position paper of a regional labour rights coalition, which was later used in consultations with ASEAN labour ministers.
To build the capacities of women´s rights organisations and movements in the region using rights-based perspectives and intersection of patriarchy, globalisation, fundamentalisms and militarisation
Through its Feminist Participatory Action Research (FPAR) programmes and thematic networks, APWLD enabled grassroots organisations to analyse how these intersecting systems shape the lived realities of women in their communities and to use that analysis to drive collective action. Organisations reported that APWLDs approach helped them move from issuebased activism to more structural, intersectional strategies that address the root causes of inequality. An example is indigenous women in Central Kalimantan, Indonesia. Through APWLDs Climate Justice FPAR programme, a local womens organisation strengthened its ability to analyse how patriarchy, global supplychain pressures, religious conservatism and militarised land control intersected in the expansion of palmoil plantations. Using the rightsbased and intersectional framework provided by APWLD, the women documented cases of intimidation, forced evictions and environmental damage linked to a company operating with support from security actors. Equipped with this evidence, they organised community consultations and presented their findings to district authorities. As a result, the government suspended the companys expansion permit, marking the first time the community had successfully halted a plantation project. Participants reported that APWLDs training gave them the analytical tools and confidence to challenge both corporate and militarised actors and to frame their demands in terms of rights rather than compensation.
No indicator available - only a description of the activity results is published
